#6207. Which Airlines Are Dry (No Alcohol)? Can You Bring Your Own Alcohol?

For many people, alcohol is an aspect of traveling by air that they enjoy. I’m not just talking about first or business class travel, where a glass of champagne might be part of the fun. Airports are also one of the few places where you can have a drink at 5AM and not be judged (too hard).

Admittedly customs differ around the globe, based on culture, religion, etc. In this post, I thought it would be interesting to talk a bit about dry airlines, as there’s a bit of nuance to this.

Which airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard? Which airlines don’t serve alcohol but let you bring your own alcohol? And does all of this even matter?

Let’s start by taking a look at the airlines that are dry, meaning that they don’t serve you alcohol. Here are the airlines that come to mind:

Admittedly that list isn’t totally exhaustive, since there are a countless number of small airlines out there. However, I think this covers the biggest and most interesting airlines that don’t serve alcohol (though if I missed any major ones, please let me know).

There’s an interesting twist to this. While some airlines are dry, they’ll let you bring your own alcohol onboard, and then you can consume it (within reason). The following three international carriers come to mind:

Now, it’s important to note that this isn’t without strings attached:

When I flew Kuwait Airways several years back, I wrote about how we brought a bottle of wine onboard, and they gladly let us consume it. It’s not that I couldn’t be without alcohol, but I was curious to experience a BYOB concept on a plane, since that was novel for me.

There’s an added layer of complexity to all of this, as there are some airlines that aren’t generally dry, but are dry on certain routes. Several situations come to mind (let me know if I’m missing any):

As you can tell, in some of the above situations, the lack of alcohol presumably has little to do with religion or concerns over behavior, and more to do with controlling costs.

People have different takes as to how “bad” it is to fly on a dry airline. On the one end of the spectrum, there are people who will avoid dry airlines at all costs. On the other end of the spectrum, you have billions of people who don’t drink alcohol at all, so this is a non-issue.

Personally I’m probably somewhere in the middle:

Regarding that last point, I do have to give credit to airlines that are dry, but still put effort into their drink selection. Take Saudia, for example, which goes above and beyond in terms of its non-alcoholic drink selection in premium cabins, with everything from cappuccinos and espressos, to excellent mocktails, to non-alcoholic wine.

Airlines often reflect their local customs and religions, so it’s not surprising that many airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard. If you definitely want alcohol when you fly, avoid airlines like Saudia. If you would like a drink when you fly, the good news is that some dry airlines actually let you bring your own alcohol, within certain limitations.

While the above doesn’t cover 100% of situations, hopefully it’s a useful, basic rundown of some of the bigger airlines that are dry.

How strongly do you feel about dry airlines? Does this policy impact your airline choice?

Travelers on United Airlines Flight 1252 from Washington to Chicago on Tuesday are in for a surprise.

They will be the first to depart from the spacious new E Gates at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), the first piece of the airport’s more than $20 billion redevelopment and the future center of United’s hub operation at the airport.

“It’s much more spacious,” Andrew Nocella, the chief commercial officer of United, said at a ribbon cutting on Monday. “The gate hold areas are large so there’s plenty of places to sit and there are all kinds of new, great restaurants to enjoy.”

In the news: United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Nocella added: “It’s the tip of the iceberg to the future development of Dulles.”

The redevelopment calls for the extension of the E Gates far to the west with room for up to 50 gates. The rest of IAD will also get a needed upgrade, including the modernization and expansion of Eero Saarinen's iconic terminal, an extension of the AeroTrain and a new international arrivals facility. The aim is to open all of this by the mid-2030s.

“This is the first step to retiring Concourse C-D [and] eliminating mobile lounges — someday," said Jack Potter, the CEO of IAD operator the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

For now, though, the focus at Dulles is on the new E Gates. They're located directly above the AeroTrain station for Concourse C. That is possible because the station was built in 2010, a long walk to the south of the existing Concourse C with the plan to eventually build a concourse above it.

Travelers coming from the train enter the E Gates in a large, high-ceilinged atrium with the new United Club immediately to their right. At 40,000 square feet, the new lounge is the second largest in United's system after the one recently opened at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

United's massive new Houston club: Inside the largest airline lounge in America

The look and feel of the lounge draws its aesthetic from the Washington, D.C., area. The entryway is inspired by the Washington Metro's vaulted subway stations; a cherry blossom mobile hangs in the central seating area; and a Blue Ridge Mountain-themed mural is painted on one of the walls.

"Lounges are very important to our customers," said Nocella. "You can see no design detail was left untouched" in the new E Gates lounge.

From the E Gates atrium, travelers make their way down the concourse itself. Gate areas are interspersed with concessions along the length. And, above, a sterile hallway takes arriving international travelers to the end of the concourse where they can board a mobile lounge to the international arrivals facility in the main terminal.

United will operate both international and domestic flights from the E Gates, Nocella said.

And, for design enthusiasts, the authority used Saarinen's original font for the gate numbers in the new concourse.

The E Gates will allow United to grow its hub at IAD. The airline plans to grow departures by about 20% next summer to around 300 daily flights, up from 250 earlier this year, Nocella said.

United will operate up to roughly 275 departures from IAD in November, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. In June 2027, the number jumps to as many as 290 a day though schedules remain in flux.

What the E Gates will not do is replace the six ground-level gates at the end of Concourse A — gates A1 to A6 — used by United Express regional jets. This was the original plan when the project was approved in the early 2020s.

Instead, United will use the new E Gates to "take the pressure off the C and D facility," Nocella said.

Potter, when asked when the airport authority will close the ground-level A Gates, said: "They’ll stay open until construction has proceeded sufficiently such that they can be relocated."

The authority aims to complete the build out of Concourse E, and the first phase of Concourse G further to the south, by 2030, Potter added.

United plans to expand its IAD hub to around 400 daily departures with all the new gates, Nocella said.

Asked when the airline would grow to 400 departures, he smiled and said they will unveil that at a "different announcement."

#6205. Flight Attendant Finds Hidden Camera In Lavatory—Passenger Charged With Trying To Erase Evidence

A flight attendant found a hidden camera in a Scoot lavatory. The passenger onboard the Singapore Airlines low cost carrier accused of putting it there is also charged with deleting evidence. It’s the deleting that creates the greatest risk of imprisonment. The incident happened October 7 on Scoot flight TR821 from Osaka to Singapore. The 52-year-old British passenger was charged in Singapore on November 5. One Mile at a Time flags the story noting he’s currently jailed. He’s now been offered S$10,000 bail. The man plans to plead guilty. According to the Singapore Police Force, the man concealed a camera in a lavatory, left, and activated recording through an app on his phone. A female flight attendant discovered the device while using the lavatory. She removed it and alerted a colleague. Police say Lutley later tried to retrieve it, found it missing, and deleted the app and related photographs to avoid detection. Officers detained him when the flight arrived at Changi Airport and seized both his phone and the camera. That’s some fancy police work! The Alleged Deletion Carries The Biggest Penalty He faces one count each of: Voyeurism: up to two years in prison, with a fine also available. Obstructing the course of justice: up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both, over the alleged deletion of the app and photographs. While the voyeurism law includes caning, Singapore exempts men over 50 so he’s in the clear there. The United Airlines Passenger Who Recorded Himself In 2019, I wrote about a United Airlines passenger accused of hiding a camera in the first class lavatory on a San Diego – Houston flight. A woman found the device and handed it to a flight attendant. The camera had recorded the man installing it. Investigators matched his clothing and jewelry to airport footage. They also recovered deleted files showing women in an Emirates lavatory, including a flight attendant. And there’s the American Airlines case where a family alleged the airline gave a flight attendant time to erase evidence after a teenage passenger discovered his phone attached to a toilet seat with maintenance stickers. Federal prosecutors later confirmed that the crewmember had reset his phone, while investigators found recordings of other children in his cloud account. He received an 18 1/2 year prison sentence last year. #6204. New Long-Haul Era: Lufthansa Receives 1st A350-1000 & 700th Airbus Jet Overall

Lufthansa has officially taken delivery of its first example of the Airbus A350-1000. The Cologne-based German flag carrier and Star Alliance founding member already flies the standard Airbus A350-900 model, and it is now starting a new era of long-haul flying as the stretched A350-1000 enters the fray. This delivery had extra significance as it also represented the airline's 700th Airbus jet overall.

The momentous occasion was marked, as such milestones often are, with a ceremony at Airbus's facilities at Toulouse Blagnac Airport (TLS) in the southwest of France. Wednesday will subsequently see the jet, which has been painted in Lufthansa's special centenary livery, undertake a ferry flight from Toulouse to Lufthansa's hub at Munich Airport (MUC) ahead of its entry into service in December.

Lufthansa confirmed in a statement that it released earlier today that its first Airbus A350-1000 bears the registration D-AIFA and the name 'Deutschland' (German for 'Germany'). As seen above, data from Flightradar24 shows that the jet concluded its pre-delivery flight test program last week, operating a 64-minute flight out of Toulouse on November 6. It did so under the French registration F-WZNY.

By the time it enters service, D-AIFA will have been fitted with Starlink WiFi, making it the first jet in the long-haul Lufthansa Group fleet to feature the new high-speed inflight connectivity solution. Carsten Spohr, the Chief Executive Officer of the Lufthansa Group, welcomed the fact that the A350 "uses up to 30% less fuel per passenger, while at the same time offering significantly lower unit costs." He added that:

"With our first A350-1000, Lufthansa is taking delivery of the world’s most modern long-haul aircraft. Our guests can look forward to the new Allegris premium cabin in all travel classes."

The delivery of the first stretched Airbus A350 to Lufthansa is the latest milestone in a long and healthy working relationship between the German flag carrier and the transnational European planemaker that dates back half a decade. On this note, Spohr said that "as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus [jet] exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa."

Today, Airbus planes form the backbone of both the narrowbody and widebody fleets at Lufthansa, which continues to fly jets from the A320, A320neo, A330, A340, A350, and even A380 families. Historically, the Lufthansa Group notes that it "has operated aircraft from every Airbus aircraft family and has served as a launch customer on numerous occasions." The A350-1000 marks the latest chapter.

Lufthansa Group Chief Executive Officer Carsten Spohr was joined at the handover ceremony by Lars Wagner, the CEO of Commercial Aircraft at Airbus, with the presence of these high-ranking executives underlining the importance of this maiden delivery. The next step will be to ferry D-AIFA from Toulouse to Munich, with this set to take place on November 11. Shortly thereafter, the aircraft will enter service.

Lufthansa's first A350-1000 has arrived with a special 100th anniversary livery, but how much paint does this livery use?

As it stands, this entry into service is set to come in the form of a long-haul rotation from Munich to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND) in Japan. This has been penciled in for Thursday, December 3, 2026. Further Asian destinations are set to be added to Lufthansa's growing A350-1000 network in the form of Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) on December 12 and Shanghai Pudong International (PVG) on December 18.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The Lufthansa Group has placed a grand total of 15 firm orders to date, of which the first ten will be used to serve Lufthansa's long-haul ops out of its Munich Airport hub. The remaining 14 examples of the type are set to be delivered by 2030, with Lufthansa saying that "the entry into service of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization program in the history of the Lufthansa Group."

#6203. AI Agents Still Need Middlemen. But Will They Need Amadeus?

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: An Amadeus office in Bad Homburg, Germany. Adobe Stock / Peter Brauers

Amadeus has the scale and airline relationships, but those advantages don't guarantee it a direct role in AI-agent bookings.

Amadeus has spent decades connecting airlines with travel sellers. AI agents may change how customers shop, but somebody still has to find flights, complete bookings, and handle changes. On its Q3 2026 earnings call on Friday, November 6, an analyst asked why Meta's Muse was using Duffel rather than Amadeus to do that work.

CFO Carol Borg said the Muse-Duffel partnership supports Amadeus' belief that AI platforms will use aggregators rather than build booking systems themselves. She doesn't think it displaces the GDS model: "It actually reinforces it."

But Duffel, not Amadeus, has the direct relationship with Muse. Other companies are pursuing similar roles across airline distribution, hotel booking and payments.

As Skift reported in September, Muse uses Duffel to access flight inv

Amadeus used its Q3 2026 earnings call on November 6 to argue that AI platforms will plug into aggregators rather than build their own booking systems, a position CFO Carol Borg said the Meta Muse–Duffel partnership "reinforces." The detail behind that claim is that Duffel, not Amadeus, holds the direct relationship with Muse, even though Duffel's inventory includes direct airline connections, NDC content, and traditional GDS inventory from Travelport. A growing set of intermediaries is taking similar positions: Selfbook powers hotel booking and payments for Perplexity, Nuitée supplies hotel booking infrastructure to Grab and Revolut and is building APIs for AI applications, Katanox has partnered with Selfbook on distribution and settlement, and AirGateway and Kyte offer API-based airline connectivity. CEO Luis Maroto pointed to roughly 3 billion daily searches and said servicing complex itineraries at that scale is harder than connecting to individual airlines. The financials show pricing holding up as volumes slip: bookings fell 2.8% in the first nine months of 2026, which the company attributed largely to Middle East disruption, while revenue per booking rose 5%. Group revenue rose 5.2% at constant currency to €5.08 billion (about $5.67 billion), with adjusted EBIT up 5.5%, and management expects full-year results near the lower end of guidance while maintaining its 2026–2028 targets.

#6202. Amex Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 175K Points Welcome Offer (Check Yours)

The American Express Platinum Card® is one of the most popular premium cards on the market, and it currently has an incredible welcome offer that’s as high as 175,000 bonus points, making it the ideal time to apply. In this post, I’d like to go over all the details of the current Amex Platinum bonus, including who is eligible, and why you might want to apply.

While the Amex Platinum has a steep annual fee, it also has compelling perks that will make it worthwhile for many, ranging from lounge access to credits. If you’re eligible for the current bonus, then picking up the card and giving it a try is a no brainer, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

The Amex Platinum Card welcome offer is potentially very lucrative, with a twist. The Amex Platinum bonus is marketed as being as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $12,000 within the first six months. However, Amex notes how the welcome offers vary, and applicants may not be eligible for that welcome offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the Amex Platinum welcome offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer, though I appreciate that Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means I value 175,000 points at a staggering $2,975, making it among the best welcome offers out there. Of course that assumes you’re eligible for this Amex Platinum bonus, which not everyone will be.

The spending requirement is significant, though you do have six months to complete it, so averaging $2,000 per month in spending might not be that hard for many people. There are lots of creative ways to reach minimum spending requirements, including things like paying quarterly taxes by credit card, if eligible.

This is potentially one of the best welcome offers that we’ve ever seen on the card, and publicly available welcome offers don’t get much better than this. In some cases people may be targeted for even bigger offers, but it’s rare. To maximize your odds of getting a targeted offer, make sure you’re opted in to getting marketing communications (by email and mail) from Amex.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to roughly 20 airline and hotel partners, and those are the best ways to get outsized value. These partners range from Air France-KLM Flying Blue, to Emirates Skywards, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer. Just to give a couple of Amex redemption examples:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Platinum Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). The primary reason you’ll want to get the card is because of the extensive perks that it offers, ranging from airport lounge access, to elite status, to credits.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

As you can see, the focus here is almost entirely on credits, lounge access, etc. When it comes to actual return on spending, the Amex Platinum isn’t very rewarding, with limited exceptions:

So this is my go-to card for airfare spending, but other than that, this isn’t a card I spend much on.

Read a full review of the Amex Platinum Card here.

The Amex Platinum Card welcome offer is huge, and is as high as 175,000 bonus points upon completing minimum spending. The structure of this offer is a little unusual, since the offer is “as high as” that amount, and when you fill out your application, you’ll see exactly what offer you’re eligible for (without an impact on your credit score).

If you are eligible for such a big welcome offer, this card is absolutely worth picking up. #6200. Military Member Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” Over Denied Free Upgrade

A military member and social media influencer has taken to Instagram to complain about a recent interaction with an Alaska Airlines employee, where he asked for a free upgrade, and was denied. He’s accusing an employee at the airline of being anti-military. Is that a fair complaint, or is this being blown out of proportion?

A military member posted a 2min35sec video online, outlining his experience with an Alaska Airlines representative at Portland International Airport (PDX), which he claims was his first time encountering an “anti-military” employee at the airline. To summarize his version of events:

You can see the video for yourself below. As you’d expect, this guy’s followers are mostly military related, so the 1,300+ comments on the post are almost entirely in agreement with the person who posted the video.

First let me say that I of course respect and appreciate the service of those who are in the military (even if I fundamentally disagree with the extent to which we get into conflicts that accomplish nothing — that’s the fault of our elected leaders, and not the fault of those who put their lives on the line).

Of course if the Alaska Airlines employee in question was rude, that’s not acceptable, and people expect polite service. Now, I’m a little skeptical of how much of a direct transcript this was, rather than how this guy chose to interpret it. That includes things like him suggesting that the Alaska employee accused him of lying. If that were the case, that’s unacceptable, but again, it’s not clear if that was actually said, or just how he was made to feel.

All that being said, this guy sort of strikes me as being rather entitled. Airlines are extremely generous with active duty military members, as they should be. The airline has a page that outlines military and veteran benefits, and upgrades isn’t among those perks. The airline offers all kinds of other things, ranging from special fares, to lounge access, to priority boarding. But it seems a little greedy to then be like “oh, they do all these things, but they should do more” (since he chooses to reference this page).

But here’s my bigger issue with this guy’s approach. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking for an upgrade, but be ready to be shot down. However, I feel like his approach is more one of entitlement than “it can’t hurt to ask.” Why do I say that?

The very example he gives is that for all these times he flies Alaska, either they say “sure, we’ll upgrade you,” or they say “sorry, it’s full, we can’t upgrade you.” In other words, he assumes he’s entitled to the upgrade as long as there are open seats, which just isn’t the policy. If he’s going to be rejected for something he’s not entitled to, he wants to be lied to, rather than told “sorry, that’s not our policy.”

And again, he emphasizes how he has no level of entitlement, but also then argues by pointing out that he has been upgraded for free in the past. It all sounds to me a little like being caught with a liquid that’s too large at the TSA checkpoint, and then trying to argue with them, and say “well last time they let me through.” Well, that’s fine, but that’s not the policy.

So my take here is that airline employees should of course always be professional. I think it’s perfectly fine to say “I’m sorry, that’s not our policy,” which is something this guy seems to take issue with. If the employee did actually accuse him of lying about being upgraded in the past, that’s of course not acceptable. But I’m also not convinced that actually happened.

A military member has accused an Alaska Airlines employee of being anti-military, after being denied a free upgrade to a seat with more legroom. He argues that there’s no harm in asking, but also seems to think that the only acceptable rejection is a claim that the cabin is full.

While Alaska offers lots of perks to military members (as they should), upgrades isn’t among them. Asking once is one thing, but I do find it a bit entitled to essentially believe that you’re entitled to the seats as long as they’re empty, and then to argue if you’re not upgraded.

What do you make of this “anti-military” Alaska employee?

Those who serve (key word: serve) in the military deserve our appreciation and respect. Their military ID is not, however, the equivalent of a premium credit card that comes with perks and benefits beyond what is directly prescribed by the US government. Someone who has chosen to serve is a laudable career decision, but it is a career decision. It is a job for which they are compensated. Meta's Muse AI agent can now book Expedia hotels in the U.S., roughly six weeks after the two companies announced the integration, but the connection is narrower than the announcement suggested. Expedia confirmed to Skift that Muse handles natural-language search and booking while cancellations and changes still route through Expedia customer support, since Expedia is the merchant of record. In a limited Skift test, Muse said it can only book properties with upfront "pay-now" pricing; pay-at-property listings require the agent to use its built-in browser on Expedia's site. Payment runs through Stripe Link, Meta's default option, even when a traveler links an Expedia account — though linking an account unlocks member pricing, which cut one listing's cost by more than $100 versus guest mode. Expedia is adding agentic channels quickly, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Google's AI Mode in the third quarter, and is packaging its technology as a B2B "template" with Qantas as the first partner. The volume isn't there yet: Expedia said it still isn't seeing meaningful traffic from AI, and Booking Holdings CFO Ewout Steenbergen said large language model referrals account for "significantly less than 1%" of Booking.com room nights. CEO Ariane Gorin said the integrations are valuable now mainly as a way to learn how agents make decisions and what tech they require, and that the small volume is high-intent traffic.

#6196. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6195. Hard Rock Hotels Plug Into Accor Without Selling a Stake

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Hard Rock keeps its equity and hands Accor the task of developing its pipeline of non-casino hotels. Accor collects ongoing fees and gets a well-known brand to essentially rent out to its loyalty members.

Earlier this year, Hard Rock International listed its hotel in New York City on Accor’s booking site and app and told almost no one.

The first month brought 84 room nights. By July, the channel was delivering more than 1,500 a month, more than Hard Rock’s own site produced for the hotel, said Jeff Hook, chief operating officer of Hard Rock. More than 90% of those guests were new to Hard Rock.

The New York hotel test was a prelude. On Monday, Accor and Hard Rock announced a global partnership. Hard Rock’s hotels will join ALL, Accor’s loyalty program. Ennismore, Accor's lifestyle joint venture, will help develop Hard Rock hotels worldwide, and Accor's global sales team will help Hard Rock win group and meetings business.

Hard Rock will have about 25 standalone hotels once the integration is fully underway, Hook said. The company also has about 10 casino hotels and three of them might eventually be listed on Accor, too.

Accor and Hard Rock International announced a global partnership on Monday that puts Hard Rock's hotels into Accor's ALL loyalty program, gives Hard Rock access to Accor's global sales team for group and meetings business, and enlists Ennismore, Accor's lifestyle joint venture, to help develop Hard Rock hotels worldwide. No equity changes hands. Accor isn't investing capital, and Chief Commercial, Digital, and Tech Officer Alix Boulnois described the structure as closer to a franchise model in which Accor is paid for the business it brings. The deal follows a quiet test: Hard Rock listed its New York hotel on Accor's site and app earlier this year, and the channel grew from 84 room nights in the first month to more than 1,500 a month by July — more than Hard Rock's own site produced for that hotel, with more than 90% of those guests new to Hard Rock, said Hard Rock COO Jeff Hook. Hook said bookings from Accor's channel are "substantially less expensive" than those from Expedia, Booking.com, or other online travel agencies. Hard Rock will have about 25 standalone hotels in the arrangement, talked to four large hotel companies before choosing Accor, and turned down offers to buy all or part of its hotel division. Ennismore's operational role will vary deal by deal, from finding development deals to full management, with casinos excluded.

Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. Some of the early reaction has been that the benefits look underwhelming. I disagree. I used to have Avis Chairman’s Club, and it was special. And American’s next-flight guarantee came through for me when I needed it, having this benefit at Alaska could be really clutch.

As one of our most valued status holders, you’ve been selected for two exceptional privileges: a complimentary upgrade to Atmos Titanium status and an inaugural membership in Atmos Global Concierge, our most elevated level of service.

The invitation emphasizes travel across Europe, Asia and Oceania, backed by a dedicated team. Global Concierge membership begins immediately and runs through December 31, 2027.

You’re invited to ATMOS GLOBAL CONCIERGE by u/iZoooom in AlaskaAirlines

Alaska is giving these customers Titanium status and Global Concierge membership.

#6192. New Bilt Deals With Hyatt, Marriott And Sports Team Reveal Bigger Bet On Rewards Across Your Whole Neighborhood

Bilt wants the building you live in, the hotel program you belong to, and the team you root for to get you recognized and rewarded at businesses around you. Its new Neighborhood OS and membership platform bring together merchants, housing communities, Hyatt, Marriott and professional sports teams in a much bigger play than earning points on rent. The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back. I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use. There are two pieces to the announcement: Tools for merchants. Neighborhood OS connects the reservation, payment, point of sale and loyalty systems a business already uses. The goal is to help it recognize customers, deliver benefits, bring in new business and encourage repeat visits. Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it. The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals! “Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent. Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry. We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched. Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest. Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert). And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants: Find customers who can become regulars. A restaurant with empty tables on Tuesday can reach people in nearby buildings who are deciding where to eat. Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full. Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people. Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount. There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. Bilt’s tech is better than what others have tried in the past. Here’s Bilt’s illustration of the merchant experience: The artificial intelligence component isn’t just buzz marketing. They can handle requests and coordinate actions across systems that otherwise require staff to do the work manually. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly. Bilt’s merchant sales page lists a $495 monthly Neighborhood OS subscription and an optional $195 monthly Neighborhood Marketplace subscription, or $690 for both. It lists a $1,500 onboarding fee waived through December 31, 2026. Bilt says members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local merchants over the last year. A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business. Sports fans. The Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury plan to launch in spring 2027 inside their existing app including concession offers, the ability to purchase seat upgrades when inventory opens, and neighborhood benefits connected to team wins. A fan concierge could help with a ride after the game or a restaurant offer nearby. Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner. Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns. Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use. Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit. I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time. Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive. They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly.

Bilt’s merchant sales page lists a $495 monthly Neighborhood OS subscription and an optional $195 monthly Neighborhood Marketplace subscription, or $690 for both. It lists a $1,500 onboarding fee waived through December 31, 2026. Bilt says members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local merchants over the last year.

A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business.

Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner.

Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns.

Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use.

Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit.

I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time.

Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive.

They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly. This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

They want to be a middleman and they’ve done payment processing for some big landlords. Exciting. Unfortunately, their 2026 was a complete disaster – dumped by a real bank, picked up by PE who wanted pie in the sky but instead got 3 versions of a credit card in 8 months that never achieved any market penetration. On the heels of that failure they’re pulling the rug out from the only part of the credit card that offered a bit more value to consumers than they could get from reliable banks.

All that means is that the marketing dollars they put into their growth plan did not result in more growth, so the marketing dollars had to be cut off because the hockey stick growth that would have supported the charade never materialized.

Now, of course, they have PE investors that would like to make some money off of this failure. So what do they do? They have some digital infrastructure that is underutilized and that they’d like to more broadly deploy. So back to basics… meaningless puffery and branding! They’re trying to refocus on the “meh” stuff that they originally did, because when pie in the sky fails, that’s what you do. Notably absent from this announcement though are any real, meaningful partnerships for “the Neighborhood OS”. Such branding and hubris.

Anyway, good news everyone, our neighborhoods are about to be brought together like never before by Bilt’s amazing AI capabilities… you know, the ones that couldn’t even answer questions about its own program accurately? In fairness, Bilt executives couldn’t answer questions about its own program accurately, so seems harsh to blame the AI.

Enjoy the grandfathering while it lasts, folks.

Frontier Airlines is about to have first-class seats.

The Denver-based budget carrier is getting ready to debut roomier seats in the first two rows of its planes. It will be a major shift for an airline long known for its tight, all-coach cabins.

And as of Tuesday, Frontier’s first, first-class tickets are officially on sale.

The airline just opened up bookings for its new front cabin, starting with flights on March 5.

However, some passengers may actually start spotting the seats even sooner, as the airline has already begun installing them on its Airbus planes.

Frontier also revealed its first true sneak peek of its new first class. The sleek black seats include a green Frontier emblem on the head rest.

They generally resemble the domestic first-class recliners you’d find on any major U.S. carriers — with one key exception: they don’t actually recline (Frontier said the seats are “ergonomically reclined.”)

TPG exclusive: Frontier wants to be an airline you'd choose to fly. Will first class and new perks do the trick?

Upgrades will be available for members who earn elite status in the carrier’s Frontier Miles loyalty program. It should be easily one of the best loyalty perks the airline has been able to offer to date.

Frontier is promising low fares for its new first-class seats, relative to competitors.

Historically, as an ultra-low-cost carrier, the airline has competed with the bigger carriers by offering lower fares.

Executives are promising a similar strategy at the front of the plane, too. “The value’s going to be there,” chief commercial officer Bobby Schroeter told TPG ahead of the announcement. “We are going to have great pricing for that type of seat that’s out there.”

Related: Frontier reports major airfare surge as high jet fuel costs pinch consumers

Beyond the two rows of first class Frontier plans to offer on all its planes, the airline is also re-configuring its extra legroom section.

You can purchase an extra legroom seat as part of Frontier's "premium bundle." Frontier also offers extra legroom access as a status perk at different tiers.

The airline is also installing USB-C ports in the first eight rows of its planes.

Today, Frontier does not have power outlets on its planes.

As part of the launch, Frontier is offering one-way $129 bundles that include the first-class seats.

It’s also selling one-way “premium” bundles for $90, which come with an extra legroom seat.

The other “first” coming to Frontier in 2027: On-board Wi-Fi. And not just any Wi-Fi.

Frontier plans to start installing Starlink service early next year on its planes. That will move its aircraft from no inflight internet service today to tech that’s widely considered the best service in the industry.

“We’re going from nothing," Schroeter noted, "to the fastest wifi in the sky."

The one question still unanswered: Whether Frontier will offer the service for free.

Complimentary on-board internet has increasingly become the norm across the airline sector. But as a budget airline, Frontier has historically charged passengers extra for most services and amenities beyond the base fare.

Executives, so far, have not shared whether customers should expect to pay fees to access its Wi-Fi.

Frontier’s rollout of first-class comes as a growing number of low-cost airlines are leaning into higher-end seats.

JetBlue plans to debut its new domestic first-class product next month. Allegiant Air will start rolling out its new seats in 2027.

The biggest long-term question for consumers: Will a flood of first-class seats into the marketplace bring down the cost of premium seating? Time will tell.

While Frontier will look to boost its bottom line by selling pricer seats, the new seats should also be a more enticing option for its loyalty members — who will now have access to true upgrades as a status perk.

The airline expects to have all its planes retrofitted by March.

#6190. Can Venezuela Build a Different Kind of High-End Tourism?

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Los Roques, an archipelago in Venezuela. Wikimedia Commons / Tucanrecords

Adriana Cisneros sees an opportunity for Venezuela to build a distinctive, conservation-minded tourism industry before the international hotel brands arrive. Whether that vision becomes reality will depend on political stability, security, and crucially, the choices made by the country's tourism leadership.

Venezuela is hardly an obvious candidate for the next great luxury travel destination. After decades of political and economic turmoil, the country faces deteriorating infrastructure, significant security risks, and an uncertain political future. The U.S. State Department advises Americans to reconsider travel, with stronger warnings against visiting several regions, including parts of the Amazon.

But Adriana Cisneros, the Venezuelan businesswoman whose family group has interests spanning media, real estate, and hospitality, believes the country has an unusual opportunity to build something different.

She estimates it could be eight years before Venezuela sees a Four Seasons, Rosewood, or Capella. Rather than waiting for the conventional luxury hotel industry to arrive, she imagines a network of four or five base camps connected by small aircraft and boats, offering access to the country's remarkable natural environments.

Adriana Cisneros, whose family group has interests in media, real estate, and hospitality, told Skift that Venezuela could skip the conventional luxury hotel playbook and build a network of four or five ultra-high-end tented camps linked by small aircraft and boats. She estimates it could be eight years before a Four Seasons, Rosewood, or Capella opens in the country, and she sees aircraft such as Cessna Caravans and Pilatus PC-12s serving remote areas rather than waiting for roads and airports to be rebuilt. This is not an announced development program. The obstacles are substantial: Venezuela's political transition is unresolved with no confirmed election timetable, the U.S. State Department advises Americans to reconsider travel and applies its highest warning to some of the remote regions central to the concept, and reliable electricity, water, healthcare, and emergency response cannot be taken for granted. Cisneros anticipates more risk-averse wealthy travelers could take another two or three years to feel comfortable visiting. The country is not starting from zero: independent operators, family-owned posadas, and lodges including Waku Lodge and Campamento Ucaima have kept tourism alive through decades of underinvestment. Cisneros points to her Tropicalia project in the Dominican Republic, where a forthcoming Four Seasons sits within a conservation-focused development, as her training ground.

#6188. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6187. Dear Robot: How Travel Is (and Isn’t) Talking to AI

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Travel brands invest deeply in AI visibility, but according to Skift's audit of 50 major travel websites' crawler policies, few tell bots where to go — and the directives don't always match who actually gets in. That looks like a shaky starting point, as the rules of AI engagement change.

Travel brands say they want AI to find them. Their websites often tell AI something else, or nothing at all.

That’s the finding of Skift’s review of robots.txt files for 50 major travel sites. These files tell automated programs, or crawlers, whether they’re welcome, and only 10 of the 50 explicitly addressed AI crawlers. The rest lumped them in with every other bot or left them to default settings.

The gap matters more as AI becomes a way travelers shop. In July, Adobe reported that AI visits to travel sites surged 119% year over year. But there’s a “major bottleneck,” according to Adobe analyst Vivek Pandya. “Significant portions of U.S. travel and retail sites remain unreadable to machines, restricting their presence across AI search results,” he wrote in a blog post.

“When an LLM cannot easily read brand content (such as amenities, pricing, or availability),” Pandya added, “potential revenue is being left on the table.”

Skift reviewed robots.txt files — the file that tells automated crawlers whether they're welcome — for 50 major travel sites and found that only 10 explicitly addressed AI crawlers. The other 40 left AI access to catch-all rules or default settings written for other purposes. That gap gained weight on Oct. 30, when Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI backed a proposal that would let a site opt out of AI training by all four with a single robots.txt entry — but only if the site adds it explicitly, since catch-all rules won't carry it. Among the sites that did set AI rules, the pattern favored visibility over training: Expedia and Vrbo give AI search crawlers broad access, Tripadvisor blocks training crawlers while allowing some search access, and Best Western and ITC Hotels explicitly welcome OpenAI's training crawler. Airbnb made the only major change in the sample, moving from allowing GPTBot and ClaudeBot in August to disallowing access across the board by October. Posted policies also diverge from enforcement: eight sites, mainly hotels, returned 403 Forbidden errors to Skift's automated requests, and CraftedStays found Marriott, Hilton, IHG, Hyatt, and Four Seasons name no AI crawler on their banned lists while their bot protection refused fetches outright. Adobe reported in July that AI visits to travel sites surged 119% year over year, and Adobe analyst Vivek Pandya wrote that significant portions of U.S. travel and retail sites remain unreadable to machines, leaving potential revenue on the table.

#6184. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6182. Expedia’s $676 Million in Acquisitions Points to More B2B Buying

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin, speaking at Skift Global Forum 2026 via remote video.  Skift

Expedia’s 2026 deals are a fraction of the nearly $6 billion it spent in 2015. But three acquisitions in nine months, plus CEO Ariane Gorin’s pledge to keep investing, signal that Expedia is a buyer again. And B2B is where the money is going.

Of the $676 million, $4 million was accrued and the rest paid in cash. The acquired companies brought $124 million of cash with them.
