#6161. MAGA panics as post-midterm investigation season looms

Among all the gruesome details of allegations both old and new of rape and sexual abuse, there’s one four-word phrase in the new congressional report on Jeffrey Epstein that says a lot about why Donald Trump seems especially unhinged these days: “No statute of limitations.” Led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released their findings on the president’s long and close relationship with the deceased sex offender. The report, citing testimony from 11 women, “indicates that Trump abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”

The media response to the allegations was muted, despite compelling new evidence about the extent of Epstein’s sex trafficking ring, suggesting more powerful men were involved than have faced legal repercussions. Perhaps the report was overshadowed by the midterm elections. Or maybe there’s a sense this is “old news” and won’t move the needle. But if Raskin has his way, we’ll all look back to this release as the opening chapter in a season of accountability not just for Trump, but also for various administration figures and MAGA cronies who have enjoyed the legal shield of a Republican congressional majority.

Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, they’ll have access to a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players.

Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, Raskin and investigators will have a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players who have been taking full advantage of the atmosphere of corruption the president has created. The Epstein report is likely just the beginning. As the Washington Post noted on Monday, Democrats “are laying the groundwork for an array of inquiries into President Donald Trump, his family and his administration.” Various business and political leaders are meeting with their lawyers, worried about what Democrats could uncover with this new power.

“I haven’t seen this much investigative activity in anticipation of a change in control of a house of Congress ever,” Michael Bopp, who runs a congressional investigations division for the law firm Gibson Dunn, told the Post.

There are plenty of signs that it’s dawning on people around Trump that he will be out of office in two short years and that, as the latest Epstein report indicates, the statute of limitations has not run out on many possible crimes committed under the White House’s protection. A recent Zeteo profile of Stephen Miller showed that the White House deputy chief of staff is worried about going to prison if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028. Congressional Democrats keep talking about impeaching Pete Hegseth, and the defense secretary is clearly anxious, reportedly making calls and begging Sen. Marsha Blackburn to appoint him to her Senate seat if, as expected, she wins the Tennessee governor’s race this week. Having a Senate seat would not only prevent impeachment; it could make prosecuting him for alleged war crimes much harder as well.

In October Elissa Slotkin of Michigan set off a massive panic on the right when she suggested that there should be a focus on “signature cases” against “people who enabled” Trump. The Michigan senator wanted a “deterrence message” for anyone considering working for Trump, letting them know that committing crimes or otherwise assisting in illegal or corrupt activity might result in “a ton of problems” for them that aren’t worth the risk of legal liability. Fox News and other outlets tried to spin this as Slotkin threatening the mass arrest of young staffers, but the hysteria belies their real worry: Democrats might be able to compile enough evidence that prison is a real threat for many of the people working for Trump.

Slotkin’s remarks clearly rattled the White House. Since then, Trump has repeatedly put out word that his underlings should not have to worry about obeying the law because mass pardons are on their way. A few days after Slotkin’s warning, sources inside the White House told the Washington Sun that administration lawyers are looking at “blanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade.”

Still, the White House is facing serious staffing issues. A September report from the Partnership for Public Service found that people Trump hires quickly leave. Not only have there been a record number of resignations, nearly half of the quitters worked less than a year for Trump.

On Monday, Trump himself also told the New York Post that widespread pardons are on the table, not just for his staff, but for allies like Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Musk has good reason to be worried. His brief tenure running DOGE has raised a whole host of questions about what laws were broken by him or by staff carrying out his orders. He’s also under suspicion of messing with Ukraine’s Starlink access, crippling its defenses against the invading Russian military. This may explain why Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars — more than any single donor in history — trying to tilt the elections in the GOP’s favor.

Trump and his family members should also be sweating. Trump has often interpreted the Supreme Court’s grant of presidential immunity as all-encompassing, but as Raskin told the New Yorker, he doesn’t see it that way at all. He outlined how the president has made billions in office, roughly $1 million a hour, and that there’s a great deal to learn about where that money is coming from. The Supreme Court’s decision technically only covers crimes committed during the commission of official presidential duties. By definition, Trump’s external money-making enterprises aren’t that. His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.

It’s tempting to wave all this off as inconsequential, because Trump and his cronies were able to escape severe ramifications the last time around. But to dismiss this talk would be a mistake, in no small part because Democrats need their feet held to the fire. The corruption this time around is far worse than it was in Trump’s first term, more flagrant as the air of lawlessness led to a level of carelessness that creates more prosecutable evidence. The next Democrat in office may not be like Joe Biden, who shied away from aggressive prosecution of Trump and his allies. Some of the politicians whose names are being bandied around — like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption.

Then there’s the matter of political will. Before now, it was hard to drum up sufficient political support for accountability because voters simply didn’t care enough about corruption. But as the New York Times reported last week, the issue is a rising source concern for voters. Democrats, for one thing, are doing a better job of linking Trump’s self-dealing to the economic problems of ordinary people. For another, the Epstein scandal has broken into national consciousness, and even Republicans are struggling to sufficiently explain why Trump, despite signing a bill to release all Justice Department files related to the case, is refusing to do so.

With these winds at their back, Democrats have a much better chance of being able to conduct thorough investigations — and pursue criminal consequences for those found to have broken the law.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Democrats lay out plans to challenge U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to the region, Paraguay’s president abruptly resigns, and Salvadoran troops deploy to Haiti.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Democrats lay out plans to challenge U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to the region, Paraguay’s president abruptly resigns, and Salvadoran troops deploy to Haiti.

The Democrats’ resounding victory in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday could spell change in the Trump administration’s approach to Latin America. It has also kicked off a debate about how the next U.S. president might approach the region.

Latin America has already received significant attention from U.S. lawmakers pushing for foreign-policy accountability for President Donald Trump. They have called for subpoenas related to Trump’s opaque oil deal in Venezuela, introduced a resolution to block deadly boat strikes in the region, and demanded hearings on deportee detentions in El Salvador.

Without legislative majorities, those efforts have moved slowly. That will change in January, when the new Congress is sworn in.

With control of Congress, Democrats could aim to “shut down” Trump’s boat strikes by attaching a funding prohibition to must-pass legislation, former State Department legal advisor Brian Finucane told FP’s John Haltiwanger. As an example of this tactic, Finucane pointed to Congress’s 1973 threat of a government shutdown to halt the U.S. bombing of Cambodia.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who will leave office in January, has said he plans to introduce articles of impeachment for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as soon as next week, unless Hegseth resigns first. Unnamed Republican sources told CNN that they expect the attempt to pass. Massie is targeting Hegseth primarily over the Iran war, alleging that the conflict contravenes the War Powers Resolution.

The defense secretary is also a vocal champion of the boat strikes in the Western Hemisphere and has said he is trying to elevate “lethality” over “legality” in military operations. Without Hegseth, the metrics for whether the United States views the strikes as a success could shift.

A bigger earthquake would be the early departure of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is steering Trump’s Venezuela policy. The Independent reported on Thursday that Rubio was “on resignation watch” as he mulled a run for president in 2028; the White House and State Department have denied the report.

Though Democrats hope their oversight will moderate Trump’s foreign policy, some analysts have argued that the opposite is possible. After Republican losses in the midterms, Trump may double down on an area where the executive branch has more leeway to act alone.

But the U.S. president could face new pushback from foreign leaders who see him as a lame duck. Right-wing Latin American presidents who have otherwise hewed close to Trump showed a taste for acting independently last week, when most swiftly recognized left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection victory. (Trump has yet to do so.)

The midterms mark the unofficial start of the 2028 U.S. presidential campaign, with prospective candidates already staffing up. Recent weeks have seen a round of think pieces by policy wonks about how the next U.S. administration should run its Latin America policy.

Last month, the Council on Foreign Relations, which has seeded staffers to both parties, published proposals that included expanding some elements of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade deal to northern South America, building out a more robust critical minerals strategy, and supporting a democratic transition in Venezuela that outlasts intense U.S. control.

On the progressive side of the spectrum, Matt Duss, a former advisor to U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, recently edited a collection of foreign-policy essays. One proposes burden-sharing on immigration policy among countries across the hemisphere. Another calls for a return to U.S. efforts to fight crime by prosecuting high-ranking white-collar criminals.

Latin America still has two more years of the so-called Donroe Doctrine to endure. But its staying power looked weaker after Tuesday.

Friday, Nov. 6, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV visits Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.

Sunday, Nov. 29: Ecuador holds midterm elections.

Riot police stand guard in front of Paraguay’s Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, on Nov. 5.Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images

Peril for Peña. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña abruptly resigned on Thursday after the collapse of a digital bank that left millions of people in the country unable to access money from their accounts. Until last year, Peña was an investor at Ueno Bank’s parent company. He named an executive linked to the bank as Paraguay’s central banker in 2023.

A series of investigations in recent weeks revealed that Ueno may have grown in prominence through connections with people in power. Regulators took control of Ueno on Tuesday.

Much of the political spectrum turned against Peña this week, even as he denied wrongdoing and said most of the bank’s customers would get their money back. On Wednesday, protesters took to the streets, including in front of the presidential palace. The next day, the top power broker in Peña’s party, Horacio Cartes, came out in support of an impeachment trial against the president.

Peña announced his resignation on Thursday shortly before being impeached, saying he was stepping aside for “the stability of our country.” Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to take over until Paraguay’s next presidential election in 2028.

Green shipping pilot. The Brazilian Port of Santos began regularly using ethanol-based shipping fuel for a small number of ships last month, becoming the first port in Latin America to do so. The move comes amid a slow global rollout of low-carbon fuels in the shipping sector—and jockeying among producers about which types of fuel will become widespread.

The International Maritime Organization aims for 5 to 10 percent of shipping fuels to come from no or low-carbon sources by 2030 as part of a draft target up for an approval vote next month. In the meantime, countries that produce biodiesel and ethanol are making the case that their fuels should be adopted as part of those efforts.

Proponents of biodiesel argue that ship engines do not need to be refitted to use their fuel, while ethanol—made from starch, corn, or sugar alcohol—requires a retrofit. That is what the cohort of ships stopping in Santos have undertaken.

Baseball’s regional roots. Last week, the Milwaukee Brewers won the U.S. baseball World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays. The final featured players born in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Venezuela, as well as the United States. It was a showcase of the sport’s deep roots in Latin America, former U.S. diplomat Steven E. Hendrix wrote in Foreign Policy.

Strained political relations between the United States and Latin American countries have often complicated baseball ties. Trump’s first-term “maximum pressure” strategy on Cuba blocked an MLB deal to ease the signing of players. And amid Venezuela’s political crisis over the last decade, many U.S. baseball academies in the country withdrew.

The Brewers’ Jackson Chourio, from Maracaibo, Venezuela, made it to the United States through a more roundabout route, first playing baseball in the Dominican Republic.

“Baseball is not a substitute for diplomacy, trade agreements, or immigration policy,” Hendrix wrote. But he argued that it shows a powerful cultural interconnectedness. In another sign that baseball has become not just America’s pastime but also Latin America’s, Venezuela defeated the United States in the World Baseball Classic in March.

Which of the following National Baseball Hall of Famers is not from the Dominican Republic?

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori walks visits the Terrorism Confinement Center in San Vicente, El Salvador, on Oct. 29. Alex Peña/Getty Images

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori was in El Salvador last week to visit the country’s Terrorism Confinement Center, a maximum-security prison known by its Spanish acronym CECOT. Her trip follows a visit last month by Costa Rican President Laura Fernández.

Both Fujimori and Fernández are expanding their own countries’ prison infrastructure in an anti-crime push. They also hope for the popularity boost that Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele experienced after he carried out a mass detention campaign beginning in 2022, targeting suspected gang members and criminals.

Now, Bukele is exporting more than sweeping detentions. He dispatched more than 2,000 security forces to Haiti over the past few weeks to fight gangs in the country, most of whom are not bound by a United Nations Security Council-approved framework that governs visiting forces.

Since 2024, Haiti’s interim authorities have welcomed international security reinforcements to help with anti-gang efforts. Many have operated under a framework approved by the U.N. Security Council, though private military contractors are also common.

Four Salvadoran troops were working under the U.N.-backed framework in mid-October when they were ambushed by Haitian gangs and disappeared. Bukele said he would send in extra forces to recover them. The prospect of a large-scale confrontation with Salvadoran troops led a Haitian gang leader this week to plea for outside mediation.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

President Donald Trump fumed at Fox News on Election Day, accusing the conservative network of turning against him, giving Democrats too much airtime and driving away its own viewers.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me.”

﻿

Trump insisted his own popularity remained strong, claiming his numbers were “better than they have ever been” and citing a CNN poll that he said showed overwhelming Republican support for him.

The president also accused Fox News of deliberately undermining him through its polling.

“The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” Trump wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLS***!'”

His grievances extended beyond the network’s programming. Trump questioned why Fox Corp. was financially supporting Democratic politicians and organizations, naming House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Reps. Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu and Pete Aguilar, along with several Democratic campaign committees. He did not provide figures to substantiate his allegations.

Trump also singled out Jessica Tarlov, the Democratic strategist and co-host of Fox News’ “The Five,” with a personal insult while watching the network’s election coverage, a complaint he brought up in previous posts.

“I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” Trump wrote, adding that he would change channels until she was off the air.

Fox News has experienced a ratings decline, although Trump’s explanation for the drop is unsubstantiated. Nielsen data showed the network’s total-day audience fell 27% in October compared with the previous year, according to TheWrap. Fox nevertheless remained the most-watched cable news network.

Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch attributed the decline to viewer fatigue during an earnings call Monday.

Trump, however, insisted the network’s coverage of him was responsible.

“They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!” he wrote. “This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

#6155. Jon Ossoff projected to handily win reelection in Georgia

Sen. Jon Ossoff easily defeated a challenge from Republican Rep. Mike Collins to hold on to his Georgia Senate seat on Tuesday, according to AP projections.

After Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, early forecasts predicted tough sledding for Ossoff. But during a brutal government shutdown — the longest on record — the senator signaled he was willing to stake his candidacy on protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies, and he proved an adept campaigner who was hyper-focused on Georgia issues. Ossoff focused his stump speeches around affordability, skyrocketing inflation and foreign entanglements, hammering Trump for his costly war with Iran.

For his part, Collins’ candidacy was hamstrung by controversies involving his payroll and affiliation with alleged white nationalists.

Frequently floated as a 2028 contender, Ossoff adopted a fighter’s stance at his campaign events. Like feisty Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the senator took every opportunity to land a jab against Republicans, occasionally causing some monocle-popping among centrist commentators still holding on to the idea of the dignity of the presidential office. In August, he drew jeers and applause for making light of the rumors surrounding Trump aide Natalie Harp.

“So [Trump] doesn’t want to do this job,” Ossoff said . “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Ossoff, for his part, has said he has “zero interest in running for president.” His victory speech, which will come later tonight, will be studied by pundits seeking to divine his intentions.

#6154. The International Power Broker Trying to Normalize Hamas

Analysis: The International Power Broker Trying to Normalize Hamas

In 2006, the last time that Palestinians voted in an election, national power broker Mohammed Dahlan fiercely opposed the new Hamas-led administration in Gaza. Dahlan has been in exile in the United Arab Emirates since 2011. But he is now setting out again to win political power in Gaza by uniting the fractious Palestinian movement—this time by including Hamas. And he is suspected of doing so with the support of influential Arab leaders and Israelis and Americans across the political spectrum.

Earlier this month, when Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed elections scheduled for November to next autumn, it wasn’t surprising. Every attempt since the last election 20 years ago has run into trouble either due to Abbas’s fear of losing or Israel’s refusal to allow voting in East Jerusalem. Fatah and Hamas, the two main Palestinian factions, clashed in 2006, which resulted in a de facto division of Palestinian territories into the West Bank and Gaza.

In 2006, the last time that Palestinians voted in an election, national power broker Mohammed Dahlan fiercely opposed the new Hamas-led administration in Gaza. Dahlan has been in exile in the United Arab Emirates since 2011. But he is now setting out again to win political power in Gaza by uniting the fractious Palestinian movement—this time by including Hamas. And he is suspected of doing so with the support of influential Arab leaders and Israelis and Americans across the political spectrum.

Earlier this month, when Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed elections scheduled for November to next autumn, it wasn’t surprising. Every attempt since the last election 20 years ago has run into trouble either due to Abbas’s fear of losing or Israel’s refusal to allow voting in East Jerusalem. Fatah and Hamas, the two main Palestinian factions, clashed in 2006, which resulted in a de facto division of Palestinian territories into the West Bank and Gaza.

Israel has exploited Palestinian divisions, citing the absence of a unified Palestinian political entity as a reason it could not move forward on peace. Most Palestinians have relentlessly called for unity among Palestinian factions. Dahlan’s party, the Democratic Reform Bloc (DRC) is now trying to achieve that elusive aim. However, including Hamas in any political alliance risks rattling Israel, which is suspected of deploying myriad tools at its disposal to influence Palestinian politics.

Born in Khan Younis, the same town as former Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, who plotted the attack against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Dahlan is seen as a son of the soil. He learned the ropes from Yasser Arafat, the architect of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), when Israel deported him to Jordan. In 1994, as the Oslo Accords were set in motion, Abbas appointed Dahlan to manage the enclave’s security as head of the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) Preventive Security organization. His reputation and reach soon earned him a reputation, and Gaza was often referred to as “Dahlistan.”

Dahlan dealt with Israeli intelligence officials and quickly made a name for himself as someone who anyone could work with. He fought against Hamas in 2006, but it was Abbas who later exiled him on corruption charges. Abbas was wary of Dahlan’s ambition and access, fearing that he might be a fierce competitor one day.

Dahlan relocated to the UAE and became a security advisor to the ruler of Abu Dhabi, Mohammed bin Zayed. He was close to the sheikh when the Abraham Accords were signed and during the military escalation in Gaza following Oct. 7, when the UAE maintained its diplomatic commitment and didn’t walk out of the deal. His proximity to Abu Dhabi’s leadership made him appealing to Israel. Could he be a Trojan horse in the Palestinian movement?

“Many Israeli intelligence officials, even those close to [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu, have met him,” said Eran Lerman, a former Israeli deputy national security advisor and retired intelligence colonel who serves as vice president of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security.

Dahlan played an instrumental role in convincing Hamas to decommission its weapons during talks with U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace—although the fate of that proposal hangs in balance as Israel demands full disarmament. Muhammad Shehada, a visiting fellow with the European Council on Foreign Relations, said that Dahlan was brought into the negotiations to build trust with Israel.

Israel has signed peace treaties with both Egypt and the UAE, and it sees them as firm opponents of the Muslim Brotherhood, a pan-Arab movement that Israel views as an ideological fountainhead of Hamas. Dahlan maintains open channels with both Abu Dhabi and Cairo, and those relationships make him an interesting figure for Israeli strategists.

In a 2024 interview with the New York Times, Dahlan laid out his vision for Palestine, declaring, “No Abbas, no Hamas,” and calling for a new generation to take charge of the PA.

Dahlan has funneled Emirati funds into Gaza, helping him revive his standing and expand his reach. He has maintained a political base through the DRC.

Dimitri Diliani, a DRC spokesperson, said that Dahlan was meeting with former Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh in Doha when the Times article was published, yet Hamas raised no objections. “That was the first sign that Hamas was willing to give up control of Gaza,” Diliani said. “But neither the U.S. nor Israel took notice.”

Hamas might accept a relegated status in Palestinian governance, but observers have questioned whether there is more than meets the eye. Some have argued that Dahlan is throwing Hamas a lifeline, ostensibly to challenge Abbas but also allowing it to survive another day as a political entity.

The DRC has formed an alliance comprising Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Fatah breakaway factions to support a unified electoral list of independent candidates to compete against Abbas. “Hamas agreed they will not participate directly and will support whatever list we announce,” Diliani said. “It will be a national list that represents us, but none of our political figures will be in it.”

That offers little comfort to Israel, which demands Hamas’s complete exit from Gaza rather than political influence by proxy. A former senior Israeli security official, who previously spoke highly of Dahlan as someone who could be acceptable to Israel to lead Gaza, now warned about his motives. The official described him as “a thief” who “can play both sides.”

Is Dahlan playing Israel, or is there a larger strategy at play behind the scenes? When asked whether he could convince Israelis to discuss a two-state solution, Dahlan struck a harsh tone. “It’s not my job to convince the Israelis,” he told the Times. “Let them go to hell.”

Adopting a firm stance against Israel remains a political necessity for any Palestinian leader—lest they be labeled as a puppet. Yet Dahlan has positioned himself as a rare figure capable of liaising between Israel, the United States, and Hamas.

Dahlan maintains he has no desire to officially run the Palestinian territories but that is standard political speak to hide real intentions. However, Lerman noted that with business ventures spanning Belgrade and beyond, Dahlan is financially well-off and may have little interest in returning to Gaza and enduring the privations that come with it.

Israel is also running out of options. It is unhappy with Abbas and sees him as ineffective in managing armed resistance, and it has called on the European Union to pressure Abbas to reform the PA and link European aid to reforms. A different version of PA reforms has been discussed in Palestinian circles. They wish to downgrade the PA, which was formed as part of the Oslo process to pave the path for a Palestinian state, and revive the PLO, which is the umbrella movement for self-determination. Palestinians argue that they didn’t get a state; instead, the PA has eroded the movement. In this vision, the PLO includes Hamas.

Diliani said that it was pointless to seek Hamas’s decimation. Even if Hamas gives up weapons, another armed rebellion will rise. “As long as Israel occupies Palestinian lands, resistance will persist in one form or another,” he said. “Dahlan has an inclusive vision.”

Israel may have to choose between Dahlan’s broader alliance that includes Hamas as a political actor or backing Abbas and his familiar operatives—such as Hussein al-Sheikh, the PA’s second-in-command, or Majed Faraj, the PA’s intelligence chief who recently called on Hamas to apologize for Oct. 7. Dahlan has a year to navigate these competing pressures and decide if he wants to jettison Hamas or risk being outmaneuvered by Israel.

#6149. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

#6147. Who Will Succeed Xi Jinping?

Analysis: Who Will Succeed Xi Jinping?

Ever since Xi Jinping bucked norms and made it clear he would not be held to a two-term limit as president of China and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), there has been intense interest in who could succeed him. Xi has purged several possible successors, but he is also aging—and even if he tries to hold onto power, he may find it easier to appoint a chosen favorite.

Although there is still no broadly recognized successor—and no such figure is likely to emerge before the CCP’s 21st National Congress late next year, if then—the intensive reshuffling of provincial officials on the eve of the Fifth Plenum may offer some clues.

Ever since Xi Jinping bucked norms and made it clear he would not be held to a two-term limit as president of China and general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), there has been intense interest in who could succeed him. Xi has purged several possible successors, but he is also aging—and even if he tries to hold onto power, he may find it easier to appoint a chosen favorite.

Although there is still no broadly recognized successor—and no such figure is likely to emerge before the CCP’s 21st National Congress late next year, if then—the intensive reshuffling of provincial officials on the eve of the Fifth Plenum may offer some clues.

On Sept. 4, Zhu Zhongming, born in 1972, was promoted from deputy party secretary of Shanghai to acting mayor, making him head of the government of China’s largest city. For a time, many observers took the move as evidence that Beijing was deliberately grooming Zhu as Xi’s future successor.

But matters are not so simple. Provincial personnel changes have since accelerated. On Sept. 23, Anhui, Henan, and Fujian all got new party secretaries. Li Lecheng and Zhou Zuyi, both born in 1965, took over Anhui and Henan, respectively, while Zhao Long, born in 1967, was promoted from governor of Fujian to provincial party secretary. (In China’s system, the party secretary is a more important figure than the governor.)

Then, on Oct. 24, two days before the Fifth Plenum opened, the pace quickened further. Wang Zhijun, born in 1965, became party secretary of Hunan, while Mo Gaoyi, born in 1964, took over in Yunnan. At the same time, younger officials moved into position for governorships: Guo Ningning, born in 1970, in Fujian; Zhuge Yujie, born in 1971, in Qinghai; and Xie Weijiang, born in 1973, in Hunan.

This reveals a clear generational shift. Provincial party secretary positions are increasingly going to officials born between 1964 and 1969, while governorships are opening up to officials born in the 1970s.

The trend becomes even clearer if we look at the officials who have already risen to full provincial or ministerial rank. Zhejiang Gov. Liu Jie, Jiangsu Gov. Liu Xiaotao, and Guangxi Chairman Wei Tao were all born in 1970. Shanxi Gov. Lu Dongliang was born in 1973. Zhu, Guo, Zhuge, and Xie have now joined this cohort. At the central level, Emergency Management Minister Zhang Chengzhong; Cheng Fubo, the chairman of China’s state-owned assets regulator; and Communist Youth League First Secretary A Dong were all born in 1970.

Only a few years ago, officials born in the 1970s were still notable enough to be labeled “young cadres.” Now they are beginning to enter the real core of senior officialdom en masse.

A candidate pool is gradually taking shape, but the real question is, what kind of person does Xi want to inherit his role? Xi’s standards for officials in general are well known: Political criteria come first; cadres must be loyal, clean, and willing to shoulder responsibility; and they must possess professional competence, a problem-solving ability, and the capacity to deal with major risks. But choosing a general secretary involves additional considerations that do not apply to ordinary senior appointments.

Discussion of Xi’s succession often falls into two extremes. One assumes that Xi cares only about loyalty. The other looks for the candidate with the strongest abilities and most complete résumé.

Both matter, but for a leader who has ruled for more than a decade and tied his own name, theory, and political line so closely to an era, the first criterion is the protection of his political legacy.

A successor must be politically reliable, but reliability does not simply mean being personally close to Xi. Xi must believe that once this person takes power, he will not repudiate Xi’s legacy. He cannot be someone who, like Nikita Khrushchev after Joseph Stalin, sucks up to his predecessor in life but denounces him in death. Nor can he be someone who, like Deng Xiaoping after Mao Zedong, preserves the status of his predecessor while fundamentally changing the system and political ideology he inherited.

The second criterion is political predictability.

An official who obeys Xi today may not behave the same way after becoming general secretary. Supreme power changes political behavior. Xi understands this better than most. As a designated successor, he was mild and cooperative with others. It was only after being granted power that he rapidly constructed a political order centered on him.

That creates a dilemma. A genuinely capable and decisive successor may eventually develop his own judgment and power base rather than remain the agent of a retired predecessor. Xi may want both: a successor strong enough to control the system and one who remains politically predictable.

The third criterion is the ability to govern.

China’s leader in the 2030s will not simply be managing GDP growth. He will have to deal with complex economic and social problems, long-term technological and geopolitical competition with the United States, possible military and security risks involving Taiwan, and a party-state containing more than 100 million CCP members, an enormous bureaucracy, complicated local interests, and a vast state-owned economy.

Someone who is loyal but incapable may ultimately be unable to preserve Xi’s political legacy. Yet someone too powerful and independent may eventually escape Xi’s influence and create a political era of his own. The successor therefore has to walk a very narrow path.

That requires experience in sensitive positions. If Xi has time to evaluate potential successors, he is likely to place the most promising candidates in different kinds of demanding posts.

This is why Beijing, Shanghai, Guangdong, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang matter. Some are economic powerhouses, some are exceptional political important, and some combine both. Running these provinces is a test, especially of performance in crisis.

Routine work, after all, matters less than how an official performs during an economic downturn, a major accident, social unrest, or a confrontation with a foreign power.

Another issue shapes the candidate pool: When does Xi intend to step down?

For several years, I have argued that Xi is likely to remain in power for another two terms, roughly from 2027 to 2037. If that judgment is correct, he has no need to choose a specific successor now.

Naming an heir too early would bring few benefits and could create a second center of power other than Xi himself. Officials would begin gravitating toward that person, while the heir’s status would give him influence well beyond his formal position. For a leader like Xi, who places such emphasis on centralized party leadership and his own dominating role, that would be an unattractive arrangement.

Xi is therefore more likely at this stage not to choose one person but to construct a pool of possible successors. All else being broadly equal, officials born between 1967 and 1975 appear to form the most realistic group to watch. If Xi hands over power around 2037, they would be between 65 and 70 years old—a plausible age range for the leadership, albeit older than either Xi or his predecessors like Hu Jintao when they took power. That might be to Xi’s advantage; an older leader would be less likely to stray from Xi’s own legacy.

I expect the age center of gravity of the 21st Central Committee to shift clearly toward those born between 1964 and 1974. Except for Xi and a small number of other top leaders, officials born in the 1950s will largely disappear from the Central Committee. Officials born in the late 1960s will become the backbone of full membership, while officials born in the 1970s will increase significantly.

If figures such as Zhao, Beijing Mayor Yin Yong, and Shaanxi Gov. Zhao Gang—born between 1967 and 1969—begin entering in significant numbers, they will naturally become important members of the top-level candidate pool for the 2030s. If post-1970 officials such as Zhu, Lu, Liu Jie, or Liu Xiaotao enter the Politburo as early as the 21st Party Congress, the signal would be stronger still.

But whatever happens, I do not believe the 21st Party Congress will clearly tell the outside world whom Xi’s successor will be. All it may tell us is who is in the final stretch of the race.

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

#6144. Andrews defeats Graham in South Carolina Senate shocker

Dr. Annie Andrews will be the first Democratic senator from South Carolina since 1998, according to AP projections. In a stunning upset, she defeated the incumbent Republican Darline Graham, who was hand-picked by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, following his death in July.

A pediatrician, Andrews positioned herself as an antidote to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA agenda. Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She described Kennedy as the “brain worm guy” and slammed Trump’s Cabinet as uniquely unsuited to their positions.

The race was never supposed to be close. South Carolina is about as red as you can imagine. The haven of cheap gas and fireworks hasn’t elected any Democrat to statewide office since 2006. Trump carried the state by 17 points in 2024.

Unlike her sibling, who shifted from staunch Trump critic to late-in-life ally, Graham was joined at the hip to the Trump administration from the outset. The president’s high disapproval ratings worked to turn the typical GOP lay-up into a closely contested race.

But Graham, a novice politician, did herself no favors. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

High early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

The Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”

#6140. Talarico, Hinojosa win big in Texas despite Elon Musk’s millions

James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

Although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

Although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

An unambiguous autocrat holds the White House. Americans now fear not only the corruption of their municipal law enforcement, but the menace of a paramilitary force of racist thugs that owes allegiance only to the executive branch. Plutocrats work hand-in-glove with white nationalists, spies have penetrated the political press, and the government prosecutes dissenting speech as treason and threatens its opponents with deportation. The year, of course, is 1916.

The cartoonist Derf Backderf has a remarkable sense of which historical moment can be mined for unfamiliar parallels to the present day. His 2020 book, Kent State: Four Dead in Ohio, arrived perfectly timed to rebut disingenuous concerns over supposed campus-activist illiberalism; his 2012 My Friend Dahmer, about his high school friendship with future serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, felt eerily attuned to a U.S. school culture traumatized by mass shootings.

An unambiguous autocrat holds the White House. Americans now fear not only the corruption of their municipal law enforcement, but the menace of a paramilitary force of racist thugs that owes allegiance only to the executive branch. Plutocrats work hand-in-glove with white nationalists, spies have penetrated the political press, and the government prosecutes dissenting speech as treason and threatens its opponents with deportation. The year, of course, is 1916.

The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! And Cartoonists!, Derf Backderf, Harry N. Abrams, 344 pp., September 2026, $29.99

The cartoonist Derf Backderf has a remarkable sense of which historical moment can be mined for unfamiliar parallels to the present day. His 2020 book, Kent State: Four Dead in Ohio, arrived perfectly timed to rebut disingenuous concerns over supposed campus-activist illiberalism; his 2012 My Friend Dahmer, about his high school friendship with future serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, felt eerily attuned to a U.S. school culture traumatized by mass shootings.

For his new graphic novel, The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! And Cartoonists!, he has identified a doozy. The book is set among leftist cartoonists working in the small-but-fierce newsroom of The Masses, the Greenwich Village magazine that published cartoons, poetry, political essays, the occasional drawing by Picasso, and at least one interview with Lenin, and that sent John Reed to cover the Bolsheviks in Moscow in October 1917. It’s a comfortable milieu for Backderf, a veteran of the U.S. alternative press for which The Masses represents a kind of platonic ideal. While the book’s dialogue is largely invented, its research is impeccable. Every time I thought, “That can’t possibly be true,” I looked it up, and it was.

The life of The Masses was short: From 1911 to 1917, it was a leading organ of U.S. socialist thought, but after the passage of the Espionage Act of 1917, the U.S. Postal Service refused to deliver the magazine on the grounds that it was interfering with conscription. The publication shut down amid punitive prosecutions of its masthead and reconstituted as The Liberator, which was milder in tone. The new magazine was thus able to print Reed’s history-making dispatches; those articles would become the basis of his book Ten Days That Shook the World, arguably the most important document in English on the October Revolution.

Covers of The Masses and Liberator.Wikimedia Commons

The eyes through which Backderf shows us all this historical detail and contemporary resonance are those of Joe Hertle, a progressive artist working for the Newspaper Enterprise Association. Hertle is Backderf’s own creation, but the NEA is still around today, syndicating comic strips and stories of various kinds to papers around the United States. Backderf imagines Hertle as a low-ranking cartoonist there, only in his mid-20s when the story takes place. He’s interested in the burgeoning labor movement—early on in the story, he loses his leg below the knee to a trolley car during a riot. But he’s also fascinated by the brilliance of the artists publishing in The Masses, which turns out some of the most beautiful U.S. artwork of the period with their illustrations and cartoons, all while dogged by a bloodlust that seems to have infected their whole society.

Backderf has an enviable array of artists to defend the radical politics he explores here. Foremost is probably Art Young, a brilliant cartoonist who clashed with his less didactically minded colleagues. “They want to run pictures of ash cans and girls hitching up their skirts in Horatio Street,” he groused in 1916, “regardless of ideas and without title.” Those colleagues were John Sloan and George Bellows, and they took the name of the Ash Can School from Young’s potshot. There’s something transcendent in the way Backderf contextualizes and reproduces obscure illustrations by future luminaries alongside Harry Ryle Hopps’ famous “Destroy This Mad Brute” military recruitment poster. What, after all, is Bellows without his comrades in the socialist press and his contemporaries in the broadsheets?

Joe Hertle, the fictional protagonist of The Dissidents, finds little sympathy for his politics in Woodrow Wilson’s United States.Abrams Books

In many respects, The Dissidents is a bracing remedial education. The villain of the piece is Woodrow Wilson, a U.S. president who is traditionally celebrated for leading the country onto the global stage during World War I and for his own academic work as a historian and president of Princeton University.

But Backderf, drawing on Adam Hochschild’s recent history of the period, American Midnight, as well as contemporaneous accounts, contends convincingly that we ignore the domestic character of Wilson’s government at our peril. He was, after all, a fervent racist who screened D.W. Griffith’s The Birth of a Nation at the White House and immediately allowed the expansion of government office segregation upon taking office—this after plying Black leaders with promises of moderation.

Wilson signed the notorious Sedition Act of 1918 and the aforementioned Espionage Act, which still plagues U.S. civil libertarians with its layers of secrecy, obfuscation, impunity, and good old bureaucratic busywork. More importantly (for Backderf’s purposes), he started a censorship board for editorial cartoonists called the Bureau of Cartoons. The bureau enlisted popular illustrators to sell the idea of censorship to their peers: One guidelines pamphlet boasted a cover by no less an eminence than James Montgomery Flagg, of the now-iconic “I Want You” poster.

Academics need to get better at reaching non-experts. Narrative media offer one possibility.

The most striking contemporary analogue in The Dissidents is that of the American Protective League, a consortium of violent goons whose existence was approved by Wilson and which was allowed to operate under color of law, despite being a club of bullies little better than the Ku Klux Klan. With Wilson’s imprimatur, they waged undeclared war on pacifists and conscientious objectors, raiding businesses and conducting arrests at their own discretion. During one three-day period in 1918, they were even allowed to conduct draft card checks throughout New York City and arrest supposed dodgers—as well as those who simply forgot to carry their draft cards with them.

In this era, too, to my surprise, segregation enthusiasts were using the not-quite-a-slur “hyphenated Americans” to refer to people who had the temerity to bring along some of their own culture when they moved to the United States. (I’ve been hearing U.S. conservatives try for laughs with this one since the 1990s.) Emma Goldman’s deportation at the end of the book feels inevitable.

All of it seems eerily similar to the 2024 Republican National Convention and its signs urging “mass deportation now” and to the work of the Department of Homeland Security’s militarized enforcement arms—Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, and Customs and Border Patrol. But Backderf places all of these familiar organizations and characters in a context so meticulously drawn—both historically and with his pen—that The Dissidents is a vivid evocation of an entire period, not just the parts that invite contemporary comparisons.

That evocation comes primarily through the art history in The Dissidents, a genuinely wonderful contribution to our shared understanding of the period. Backderf’s own style is deliberately prosaic, with lots of heavy black ink, but the artists he’s chosen for his cast of characters often use a black crayon, and Backderf includes stats of their cartoons on his own pages; these bring forth a whole range of values seen nowhere else in the book’s world.

Joe admires the provocative political cartoons in The Masses.Abrams Books

Backderf takes great pains to dramatize all the different layers of artistic expression available to the general public during World War I, and how they changed in response to social pressures. To avoid seeming too sympathetic to the Germans, The Katzenjammer Kids and Hans und Fritz, both created by Rudolph Dirks, were renamed The Shenanigan Kids and The Captain and the Kids, respectively.

Cartoonist Art Young drew scathing indictments of capitalism, official impunity, and even the Associated Press; he was charged under the Espionage Act and put on trial, through which he snoozed defiantly. Other Masses contributors weren’t as lucky: For organizing French railway workers to strike, Robert Minor was imprisoned abroad by the U.S. military and narrowly avoided being executed; Maurice Becker, arrested for being a conscientious objector, was held and tortured at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, a military prison in Kansas.

The rest of the press seemed to consider these men to have gotten off easy. “We are now at war, and militant pacifists are earnestly reminded that there is no shortage of hemp or lamp-posts,” snarled the Wall Street Journal in a bravely unbylined front-page editorial on April 6, the day the United States formally entered the war. This, too, evokes more recent memories of the U.S. press disciplining its less hawkish members. (The Journal recently published an letter under the delightfully petulant headline “The Iran War Isn’t Deranged.”)

Undergirding the eeriness of its parallels, depending on how depressed you’ve been lately, you might find in The Dissidents a sense of relief. I certainly did. It’s not that things aren’t terrible, but it’s worth remembering that they’ve been bad before and gotten better (and worse) as the passage of time has done its thing. If it’s not exactly a comfort to feel that somewhere in the U.S. character there lurks a penchant for thuggery, it is at least nice to think that, for long periods, its expression has been curbed and limited. “Things don’t last forever, Joe,” the great, subtle artist Cornelia Barns tells our hero, as the net begins to tighten around the radical journalists of The Masses. And that’s true enough, for good and for ill.

#6134. MAGA wiped out in blue avalanche

The signs were there from the outset. About 30 minutes after the polls in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District closed at 6 p.m., the first numbers from rural counties began trickling in. It was no surprise that they favored Republican Ralph Alvarado over Democrat Zach Dembo. The district was reliably Democratic until 2012, when Andy Barr, a Republican who is now running to replace Mitch McConnell in the Senate, eked out a win. Since then, the GOP has gerrymandered the district to all but ensure it stayed in the fold.

The real story, though, could be found in the margins. Alvarado was underperforming Barr’s 2024 results by around 20 percentage points — a staggering drop, indicating that a significant number of Republicans had either stayed home or decided to take a chance on Dembo. Off the Democratic map for the last 14 years, by 9:15 p.m., when it was reported that Alvarado had conceded, the district had become a microcosm of what was unfolding nationwide.

The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.

Further south in Georgia, an earlier-than-expected call for Jon Ossoff buoyed Democratic hopes, followed by a pickup in the North Carolina Senate race, which saw Gov. Roy Cooper projected to defeat former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. Democrats even put up a fight in ruby-red Florida’s statewide races, with David Jolly, the nominee for governor, and Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist Senate candidate, running ahead of their opponents until the conservative Panhandle’s votes were counted.

Then came South Carolina, where Darline Graham, who was foisted upon the state’s Republican Party by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his death, went down to an historic defeat. The Palmetto State hasn’t seen a Democrat elected to the Senate since 1998.

Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, routed her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after he released a widely condemned ad that weaponized a horrific part of her childhood. In Texas, James Talarico is projected for a stunning win over scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion.

Other elections around the country — Senate races in Michigan, Kansas and Iowa; pivotal House contests and gubernatorial races — appear to be trending for Democrats.

For a decade, the party has wondered when, or if, a reckoning would arrive for Trump and MAGA. That moment has arrived.

Again and again, Republicans have followed the president over the cliff, no more so than during the past 22 months. In 2024, Trump expanded on the coalition that had carried him to success in 2016 by making inroads with Black men, Latinos and young voters. It was a success that, at least in part, led Republicans to launch a national gerrymandering scheme largely thwarted by Democrats, as well as an unfavorable economic climate of the president’s own making.

But Trump also made the grievous error of attacking the very communities that helped return him to the White House. The combination of his assaults on voting rights and Black history, as well as the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, ensured that Black voters turned out overwhelmingly for Democrats. After more than a year of ICE raids, mass deportations and threats against naturalized citizens, Latinos have swung to the Democrats en masse, playing a decisive role in Talarico’s win. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

The monumental defeat suffered by Republicans offers a sobering lesson for Democrats — to not forget what brought them to this night of victory.

The message voters are sending is loud and clear: They want fighters, leaders who are willing to throw out conventional wisdom and do battle for working-class interests. That’s what Ossoff sensed last fall, when he was considered to be the nation’s most endangered Democrat. Instead of playing it safe, he staked his candidacy on affordability issues, particularly subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. In the midst of the longest government shutdown on record, Ossoff held firm: He would not vote to reopen the federal government unless the tax credits were restored.

Other Democratic candidates got the message. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan proved steadfast in linking the billions in federal funding that continue to subsidize Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza to skyrocketing consumer prices on the homefront. Another physician, Dr. Annie Andrews, who defeated Graham, unabashedly campaigned on creating a healthcare public option and gun control measures in South Carolina — and won.

Right now, Democrats are feeling the wind at their backs. But after the excitement fades from tonight’s successes, they will realize they are now facing an even bigger challenge: To stay true to the mandate they have been given by voters, grudgingly in some cases, and to not, as they have done so often in the past, slip on the proverbial banana peel that is always waiting for them around the corner.

Throughout his campaign for the Senate, Paxton was fond of saying, “If we lose Texas, we lose America.” Tonight, Democrats put Texas solidly in their column — and America is still standing.

#6130. Donald Trump is now radioactive

Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks. Millions of voters did exactly that. Be careful what you wish for, my dude.

The astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump. Those neutral-sounding terms of art are not remotely adequate. This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. It represents this nation’s collective awakening — admittedly rather late in the game — to this individual’s uniquely poisonous effects on our public life and civil society.

Many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump. They will lose his number. They will profess that they were never convinced MAGA believers, or that they secretly disagreed with the ICE reign of terror, with the war in Iran, with the disastrous tariffs, with the ideological assault on liberal democracy.

Is JD Vance still a plausible 2028 presidential contender, having hitched his wagon to this tyrant, who has now been thoroughly pantsed in public and exposed as a pathetic loser? Will Pete Hegseth get even one more opportunity for podcaster-style flexing before the defanged Pentagon press corps? Let’s give Marco Rubio an infinitesimal amount of credit for creeping quietly through the corridors of power and staying out of the headlines. Whether his neocon mouse act is enough to survive the Trumpocalypse moment remains to be seen.

In his inimitable style, Trump is already blaming others for this defeat. He has accused Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday night’s numerous shockers — of being a RINO sellout. As impossible as it is to talk about honor with these people, that is an act of dishonorable treachery, given how eagerly Abbott has crawled and begged and prostrated himself before the Trumpian throne.

Then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didn’t do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. It only made the problem worse — all the problems, really — and they should have seen that coming.

The president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. I’m not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him — its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing — and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

We don’t know how this election would have turned out in the unimaginable alternate universe where Trump stayed out of it. But he didn’t. He forced Sen. John Cornyn out of the race in Texas, in favor of Ken Paxton. Look what happened. He picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina. Look what happened. He picked Mike Collins to run against Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and Michael Whatley to run against former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina. Look what happened. He praised Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

And that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the New York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

Are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

That’s about where we are. Trump has always been poisonous. Republicans are finally learning that the hard way.

#6124. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

This article was originally published on The Conversation.

Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”

The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”

For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

And that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”

And then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”

Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

Trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison
